{"concepts_used":["GC-0055","GC-0053","GC-0001","GC-0002","GC-0004","GC-0007","GC-0008","GC-0009","GC-0072"],"decline_reason":"","declined":false,"citations":[{"ref":"TMA1995/s39(2)","quote":"(2) An application for the registration of a trade mark may be rejected if the trade mark contains or consists of:"},{"ref":"TMA1995/s39(2)(a)","quote":"(a) a sign that is prescribed for the purposes of this subsection; or"},{"ref":"TMM/Part31/3#1~1","quote":"As such, and taking into account the presumption of registrability, a ground for rejection will generally only be appropriate under subsection 39(2) if a trade mark contains or consists of one or more of the signs prescribed and the presence of that sign would be likely to confuse the relevant public as to whether: the goods and services bearing the trade mark have a particular status given by legislation, or there is a connection between the applicant and the person, body, or organisation with whom the sign is associated."},{"ref":"TMA1995/s43","quote":"An application for the registration of a trade mark in respect of particular goods or services must be rejected if, because of some connotation that the trade mark or a sign contained in the trade mark has, the use of the trade mark in relation to those goods or services would be likely to deceive or cause confusion."}],"answer":"Yes, generally—as a matter of Manual practice, but not as an express statutory requirement under section 39(2).

**The Act:** Section 39(2)(a) permits rejection where a trade mark contains or consists of a prescribed sign. It says “may”, and the supplied wording does not expressly require a likelihood of deception or confusion. [TMA1995/s39(2); TMA1995/s39(2)(a)]

**Manual practice:** The Registrar will generally only raise this ground if the prescribed sign would be likely to confuse the relevant public about either the goods or services having a particular legislative status, or a connection between the applicant and the person, body or organisation associated with the sign. This practice takes account of the presumption of registrability; the sign’s presence alone is therefore generally not enough under that guidance. [TMM/Part31/3#1~1]

**Separate statutory ground:** Section 43 requires rejection if a connotation of the mark, or a sign within it, makes use for the specified goods or services likely to deceive or cause confusion. That is a likelihood test, not a requirement to establish that consumers have already been deceived or confused. [TMA1995/s43]"}
